title: How To Respond To Subpar Class Performance https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2018/05/12/how-to-respond-to-subpar-class-performance/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin warns against the natural instinct to lower expectations after a class delivers a subpar performance, arguing that even a small easing of standards signals that the teacher didn't really mean what was said and that sloppiness is acceptable. Instead, he recommends letting the underwhelming activity play out fully so students experience what poor performance feels like, then pausing for their attention and reteaching the same activity at an even higher level of detail and expectation than before. He explains that asking for more, not less, in the moment right after a poor performance has a shocking, re-motivating effect on students. The reteaching should be highly detailed and enthusiastic, followed by genuine, earned praise once students demonstrate they can meet the raised bar. He frames every subpar moment as an opportunity to strengthen the class rather than a reason to worry or relax standards.
points: Lowering standards after a subpar performance, even slightly, signals that the teacher doesn't mean what they say.
The recommended response is to let poor performance play out fully rather than intervening immediately.
Reteaching should raise the bar—asking for more or better than before, not simply repeating the original expectation.
Asking for a higher standard immediately after a lapse has a re-motivating, almost shocking effect on students.
Genuine, earned praise after the reteaching reinforces the higher standard as a powerful motivator.
quotes: Because loosening of standards—even a tad—always, immediately, and effectively lowers the bar of what is considered “good” in your classroom.
It tells students that you don’t really mean what you say and that sloppiness and carelessness are a-okay.
So, the best response is to first wait until the less-than-acceptable activity plays itself out. Let your students experience what poor performance feels like. Let them live in it.
After another long pause, launch into a reteaching of the same activity but now with an even greater level of detail and expectation.
There is something about asking students to meet an even higher standard in such moments that shocks them back into right behavior.
Crank up your expectations, reset the bar on a higher rung, and those subpar moments will rarely, if ever, happen again.
